title: Proof
body:
[[Proof By Induction]]
[[Proof By Contradiction]]
[[Direct Proof]]

A **proof** is an argument that a claim holds in *every* case covered by the claim. It is
not evidence and it is not testing. One counterexample destroys a universal claim; no
number of confirming examples establishes one. That asymmetry is the reason the technique
exists, and it is the habit [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]] runs entirely on.

## Picking the technique

The shape of the claim tells you which one to reach for.

| Claim looks like | Technique | Why |
|---|---|---|
| "if $A$ then $B$" | [[Direct Proof]] | Assume $A$, walk to $B$ |
| "no such thing exists", "not regular", "irrational" | [[Proof By Contradiction]] | A negative has nothing to construct, so assume it is false and break something |
| "for all $n \ge 1$ ..." | [[Proof By Induction]] | Infinitely many cases, indexed by the naturals |
| "for all recursive structures ..." | structural [[Induction]] | Same thing, indexed by how the object is built |
| "$A = B$" for sets | double inclusion | $A \subseteq B$ and $B \subseteq A$, see [[Sets]] |
| "there is some $x$ with ..." | direct, by construction | Exhibit one and check it |
| "not every $x$ has ..." | counterexample | Exhibit one that fails; that is a complete proof |

Contradiction and contraposition are worth keeping apart. Contraposition proves
"if $A$ then $B$" by proving "if not $B$ then not $A$", which is the same statement.
Contradiction assumes $A$ **and** not $B$ together, and derives something impossible.

## Standing rules

- State what you are assuming and what you are proving, before you start.
- "Arbitrary" is load-bearing. Choosing an arbitrary $x$ is what makes the argument cover
  all of them; choosing a specific $x$ proves nothing general.
- Say where each step comes from: hypothesis, definition, or a previous line.
- $\blacksquare$ or $\square$ at the end. Say where you finished.

## Where this is used

- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]] is the most proof-heavy COMP course in the degree. The
  [[Pumping Lemma]] and the halting argument in [[Turing Machine]] and [[Undecidability]]
  are both [[Proof By Contradiction]]; the [[NFA]] to [[DFA]] construction is an induction.
- [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]]: proving a bound in [[Asymptotic Analysis]] and proving a
  recursive structure correct.
- [[INTRODUCTION TO SOFTWARE ENGINEERING]] is the contrast worth noticing: [[Unit testing]]
  samples the input space, a proof covers it. Testing shows the presence of bugs, never
  their absence.

- [[Systems of Logic]] in [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]] is the same subject from the other end.
  These notes are about convincing a reader; that one is about what happens when the rules are
  made mechanical enough to hand to a machine, and it is where $\vdash$ (provable) and $\models$
  (true) come apart. [[Godel's Theorem]] is the punchline.
